list.listitem: Consider the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) in asymptomatic patients with fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥126 mg/dL, 2-hour plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL after a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or hemoglobin A1c ≥ 6.5%; or in patients with hyperglycemic symptoms with random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL. B

The American Diabetes Association (ADA) defines prediabetes as FPG of 100 mg/dL to 125 mg/dL, OGTT of 140 mg/dL to 199 mg/dL, or A1c of 5.7% to 6.4%. The World Health Organization (WHO) has a similar definition except for FPG of 110 mg/dL to 125 mg/dL. Prediabetes, rather than a diagnosis, is a risk factor for T2DM and cardiovascular disease, conferring a continuous risk even below stated thresholds and a significantly elevated risk at the higher range. B

Screen nonpregnant adults between ages 35 and 70 years with BMI ≥25 (or ≥23 for Asian Americans) for T2DM or prediabetes (USPSTF). B Alternatively, consider screening all adults 35 years and older, or any adult with BMI ≥25 (or ≥23 for Asian Americans) with 1 or more risk factors, and consider rescreening every 3 years (ADA). C
Screening asymptomatic patients for T2DM does not appear to affect all-cause mortality or cause-specific mortality. B

For prediabetic patients with BMI ≥25 (or ≥23 for Asian Americans), intensive lifestyle interventions or metformin reduces the incidence of T2DM and improves intermediate outcomes (eg, weight, BMI), but has not been shown to improve mortality or long-term cardiovascular outcomes. A
Statin therapy and smoking cessation reduce complications and mortality in patients with T2DM and should be primary treatment goals. A

Blood pressure should be lowered to less than 140/90 A based on JNC-8, or less than 130/80 C based on ACC/AHA and ESC/ESH guidelines. A systolic blood pressure target of 120 mm Hg produces no additional cardiovascular benefits versus 140 mm Hg and increases harms. B

A hemoglobin A1c target between 7% and 8% appears reasonable for most patients with T2DM, but glycemic targets need to be individualized based on patient preference, comorbidities, polypharmacy risk, and life expectancy. Patients, especially older adults, who stay within their individualized A1c targets ≥60% of the time have lower all-cause mortality and cardiovascular complications than those who remain below and/or above their individualized targets ≥60% of the time. More intensive glycemic targets may reduce microvascular complications but this is of questionable significance. B

Metformin is the preferred agent for initial monotherapy for most patients, based on mortality benefit, side effect profile, and cost. Its mortality benefit appears independent of its glucose control. B

Sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists reduce major cardiovascular events (nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, and CV mortality) and all-cause mortality in diabetic patients with established cardiovascular disease, independent of glucose control. A

SGLT-2 inhibitors improve renal outcomes (composite endpoint: 50% reduction in GFR, progression to ESRD, dialysis, renal death) and all-cause mortality in patients with macroalbuminuria or chronic kidney disease (CrCl 30-90 ml/min), and decreases hospitalization for heart failure in patents with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). A
In T2DM, self glucose monitoring does not meaningfully improve A1c levels or reduce complications, and may increase adverse events. A

background.definition: Diabetes mellitus type 2 is a chronic disease of hyperglycemia due to a progressive insulin secretory defect in the setting of insulin resistance.

list.listitem: As of 2019, approximately 37.3 million (11.3%) U.S. adults had type 2 diabetes. An estimated 8.5 million of these adults were undiagnosed. The prevalence increased with age, with 24.4% of adults age 65 or older having diabetes.

Although the overall prevalence of diabetes is increasing, likely due to better treatments and longer survival, there was a decrease in the incidence of newly-diagnosed diabetes in adults from 2008 (8.4 per 1000) to 2018 (6.9 per 1000), suggesting that preventive approaches may be working.
In 2017, the US healthcare system spent an estimated $327 billion on direct and indirect medical costs for people with type 2 diabetes.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus was the 8th leading cause of death in 2020 in the United States.
Obesity, overnutrition, inactivity, inflammatory states (including those triggered by obesity), and genetic factors contribute to insulin resistance and the development of type 2 diabetes.
Insulin stimulates glucose uptake in various tissues throughout the body.
Tissue insulin sensitivity is regulated by multiple genetic variants at multiple loci. As of 2019, there are 243 genetic loci associated with type 2 diabetes risk.
Blood glucose levels are regulated by multiple endocrine hormones, including insulin, glucagon, and GLP-1.
A confluence of many factors (genetic and environmental) mediates development of insulin resistance, leading to rising insulin levels.
Initially, the pancreatic beta cells increase insulin production to overcome insulin resistance and maintain euglycemia. Eventually, beta cells fail and hyperglycemia results.
Microvascular and macrovascular diseases occur, which may result from hyperglycemia or other metabolic changes.

Screen nonpregnant adults between ages 35 and 70 years with BMI ≥25 (or ≥23 for Asian Americans) for T2DM or prediabetes (USPSTF). B Alternatively, consider screening all adults 35 years and older, or any adult with BMI ≥25 (or ≥23 for Asian Americans) with 1 or more risk factors, and consider rescreening every 3 years (ADA). C .
Screening asymptomatic patients for T2DM does not appear to affect all-cause mortality or cause-specific mortality. B

For prediabetic patients with BMI ≥25 (or ≥23 for Asian Americans), intensive lifestyle interventions or metformin reduces the incidence of T2DM and improves intermediate outcomes (eg, weight, BMI), but has not been shown to improve mortality or long-term cardiovascular outcomes. A

The USPSTF recommends screening for T2DM and prediabetes in patients aged 35 to 70 years with BMI ≥25 (or ≥23 for Asian Americans). Consider earlier screening in higher-risk populations (Black, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander).

The American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommends screening asymptomatic adults every 3 years starting at age 35 years. They also recommend screening adults of any age with a BMI ≥25 (or ≥23 for Asian Americans) and at least one risk factor (see for risk factors). Screening can be repeated earlier with new symptoms or weight gain. At least annual screening is recommended for those with prediabetes by the ADA. In children/adolescents, they recommend screening if the child is overweight (BMI ≥85th percentile) or obese (BMI ≥95th percentile) and one or more pediatric risk factors are present ().
The ADA recommends use of validated risk calculator (https://diabetes.org/socrisktest) or informal risk factor assessment to guide screening for prediabetes and T2DM in asymptomatic adults.

Based on a British study of predominantly Caucasian patients, the number needed to screen (NNS) to diagnose T2DM or prediabetes varies depending on assigned cutoffs for age and BMI. For an English population older than 50 years with a BMI>27, the NNS ranges from 15 to 28.

Screening asymptomatic patients for T2DM or prediabetes does not appear to affect all-cause mortality or cause-specific mortality (ie, cardiovascular, cancer, diabetes-related, and other mortality), based on limited evidence from systematic review (2 RCTs; n=25,120) for the USPSTF.

The same USPSTF systematic review evaluated 5 RCTs enrolling 5,138 participants and concluded that, for prediabetic patients with BMI ≥25 (or ≥23 for Asian Americans), intensive lifestyle interventions or metformin reduces the incidence of T2DM and improves intermediate outcomes (eg, weight, BMI).

In patients with impaired fasting glucose (IFG) and impaired glucose tolerance (IGT), the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) trial showed intensive lifestyle interventions (≥7% weight loss goal through low-calorie, low-fat diet and moderate-intensity physical activity of at least 150 minutes per week) reduced the incidence of diabetes over 3 years by 58% (NNT 7). Metformin reduced incidence of diabetes by 31% (NNT 14) over 3 years, but was inferior to intensive lifestyle changes.

A long term (median 21 years) open-label follow up of the DPP trial found no reduction in mortality or cardiovascular events in either the intensive lifestyle intervention or metformin groups compared to usual care. Other systematic reviews and meta-analyses have also failed to demonstrate that lifestyle changes or metformin improves long-term cardiovascular or mortality outcomes.

The effect of intensive lifestyle modification interventions to prevent diabetes are sustained for 5 to 15 years after the intervention is stopped, but this effect wanes with time and may be at least partially dependent upon ongoing lifestyle management support.

A 2023 meta-analysis demonstrated that exhibiting healthful behaviors such as healthy body weight, healthy diet, regular exercise, and smoking cessation/abstinence are associated with a lower likelihood of developing T2DM. However there is insufficient evidence to suggest that counseling patients to follow these lifestyle recommendations will decrease their risk of developing T2DM.
There is lack of moderate- and high-certainty evidence that either diet alone or exercise alone prevents T2DM and its complications in patients with IGT or IFG.

In patients who are overweight or obese, behavior-based weight loss interventions reduce the absolute risk of developing T2DM by approximately 14.5% over 3 to 9 years (NNT 7). Based on moderate-certainty evidence, the USPSTF recommends that clinicians offer or refer adults with obesity (BMI ≥30) to intensive, multicomponent behavioral interventions as this leads to higher weight loss and lowers the incidence of T2DM compared to usual care. However, there is no firm evidence that intensive behavioral interventions improve mortality or cardiovascular outcomes nor lead to long-term weight loss.

Referral sites for the National DPP can be found at www.cdc.gov/diabetes/prevention/find-a-program.html. Eligibility requires patients have an overweight BMI and be at risk for diabetes based on laboratory testing. Many states have established or expanded Medicare DPPs.

Among at-risk older adults, a calorie-reduced Mediterranean diet (by 600 calories per day) combined with intensive, ongoing support and increased physical activity over 6 years can decrease the incidence of diabetes compared to a Mediterranean diet without calorie restriction (NNT = 40), based on a study of 4,746 adults with metabolic syndrome without diabetes or cardiovascular disease.

Based on moderate-quality evidence from a Cochrane review, metformin appears better than placebo and non-intensive lifestyle (diet & exercise) interventions, but no better than intensive lifestyle interventions in reducing the incidence of T2DM among patients with prediabetes. Metformin's effects on mortality, macrovascular, microvascular, and health-related quality of life outcomes for patients with IFG or IGT are uncertain.

Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors prevent or delay the onset of diabetes in patients with IGT, based on very low- to moderate-certainty evidence from a Cochrane review. The strongest data was of moderate certainty, and was for acarbose vs placebo (NNT 28).

In a meta-analysis limited by heterogeneity, weight loss medications (orlistat, phentermine/topiramate), insulin sensitizers (metformin, pioglitazone, rosiglitazone), alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose, voglibose), valsartan, bezafibrate, and glargine, appear to decrease the incidence of T2DM in patients with prediabetes during the active treatment period. After discontinuation (average follow-up 17 weeks post-intervention), the effects of these medications appear to wane.

Pioglitazone may delay the diagnosis of diabetes compared to placebo (low-certainty evidence) and compared to no intervention (moderate-certainty evidence), but sustained effects after discontinuation are uncertain. It may cause weight gain and edema.

In patients with obesity, low-quality evidence suggests that liraglutide, lorcaserin, naltrexone/bupropion, orlistat, and phentermine/topiramate may prevent development of type 2 diabetes at 4 years of follow up. These results were limited by high dropout rates but were consistent across 3 trials with >9000 participants. The USPSTF did not find sufficient evidence to include this in their recommendation statement.
There is insufficient evidence for the efficacy of insulin secretagogues like sulfonylureas and meglitinide analogues in preventing T2DM in patients with prediabetes.
Given the lack of RCTs, a Cochrane review found uncertain evidence for the effectiveness of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors in preventing T2DM and its complications.

Tirzepatide appears effective in decreasing weight and the incidence of T2DM among patients with prediabetes and obesity (NNT = 8 over 3.4 years). We do not have data yet whether tirzepatide and similar medications improve mortality and cardiorenal outcomes for this population.
Hormone therapies (estrogen and progestin) do not appear to lower the incidence of diabetes in patients with prediabetes.

In an RCT involving 2,423 patients with prediabetes, vitamin D supplementation did not decrease the incidence of T2DM in patients with normal or mildly low vitamin D levels. In post-hoc sensitivity analysis from a meta-analysis of moderate quality, vitamin D supplementation ≥1000 units daily in patients with prediabetes had a very small but statistically significant preventive effect. A meta-analysis using individual patient data from 3 RCTs evaluating 4,190 adults (mean age 61 years) with prediabetes concluded that vitamin D supplementation (cholecalciferol 20,000 IU/wk or 4,000 IU/d, eldecalcitol 0.75 mcg/d) is superior to placebo over a median of 3 years in preventing T2DM (NNT = 18-115), with the benefit more pronounced in patients who achieve vitamin D levels ≥50 ng/mL. Adverse events appeared similar between treatment and placebo groups (eg, nephrolithiasis, hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, death), but the trials may have been underpowered to identify a difference.
Omega-3 (dietary or supplemental) does not prevent development of T2DM (moderate-quality evidence).
Evidence for alpha-linolenic acid, dietary polyunsaturated fat, and omega-6 is of low- to very low-quality and inconclusive.

USPSTF recommends statin therapy for primary prevention for patients with T2DM 40 to 75 years of age without existing cardiovascular disease (CVD) with an estimated 10-year CVD risk ≥10%, based on moderate-certainty evidence. Statins decrease all-cause mortality and CVD events across diverse clinical populations and demographics.

Metformin, SGLT-2 inhibitors, and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists all offer mortality benefit, though metformin's effect was not confirmed in recent meta-analyses. Meta-analyses conflict on an individual drug level regarding mortality and prevention of other complications.

The ADA recommends low-dose aspirin in patients with T2DM plus increased cardiovascular risk but without a diagnosis of ASCVD, assuming a shared-decision making conversation has taken place regarding risk versus benefit (A recommendation). However, the ASCEND trial showed no difference in the originally defined composite vascular primary outcome between placebo and aspirin groups. Adding TIA to the composite vascular outcome resulted in slight benefit, with NNT = 90 over 7.4 years. Adding revascularization to the composite vascular outcome also revealed slight benefit, with NNT = 77 over 7 years. The NNTH = 111 for the composite outcome of major bleeding events. Patients with T2DM and ASCVD should be treated with low dose aspirin, barring contraindications, as benefit vs risk margin is greater in this population (ADA, A recommendation). ESC/EASD 2019 guidelines recommend against aspirin use for primary prevention in patients with T2DM, though it can be considered in patients at high or very high risk of cardiovascular risk and no contraindications. Please see the Drug Therapy subsection for more information.
See and the Therapy section for additional information about medications that mitigate diabetes-related complications.
Please see Therapy: Management of Complications subsection for use of medications to prevent worsening of nephropathy.
Blood pressure control reduces diabetes-related complications and deaths in a cost-effective manner.

Tight glucose control slightly reduces microvascular surrogate events (retinopathy detected on screening, and nephropathy), but does not reduce macrovascular complications (such as myocardial infarction and stroke) or clinical microvascular outcomes (vision impairment, end-stage renal disease, peripheral neuropathy, etc.). Tight glucose control does not improve all-cause mortality rates or quality of life, and may worsen mortality.

However, for recently diagnosed T2DM (not screen-detected), intensive glucose control with metformin (compared to usual care) in overweight adults appears to decrease all-cause mortality 10 and 20 years post-randomization. Intensive glucose control with sulfonylurea or insulin for recently diagnosed T2DM (compared to usual care) lowers all-cause mortality only at 20 years, but not 10 years, post-randomization. This data is from the updated evidence report and systematic review for USPSTF on screening for prediabetes and T2DM.
Follow Centers for Disease Control recommendations for adult vaccinations specific to patients with diabetes.
Omega-3 supplementation (1 gram daily) does not reduce all-cause mortality or composite vascular outcomes in patients with diabetes.

Fasting plasma glucose, 2-hour oral glucose tolerance testing, and hemoglobin A1c are all acceptable diagnostic tests for T2DM. If symptoms of hyperglycemia (polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, etc.) are present, a random glucose ≥200 is sufficient for diagnosis. Hemoglobin A1c is the least sensitive but most pragmatic of the diagnostic options for asymptomatic patients.

The ADA recommends repeating the test for confirmation of the diagnosis. Either repeating the same test at a future time or ordering one of the other diagnostic tests from the same blood sample is acceptable.

Diagnostic criteria for states of abnormal glucose metabolism indicating future risk of diabetes, cardiovascular events, and microvascular complications have changed over time and vary by organization, with the ADA endorsing the lowest glucose cut-offs. Terminology (prediabetes, impaired glucose tolerance, impaired fasting glucose) also vary by organization. Inconsistent definitions impair precision of risk prediction based on one of these diagnoses. Using the ADA definition, prediabetes may be under-diagnosed and under-treated in primary care settings.

Unlike patients with type 1 diabetes, many patients with type 2 diabetes are asymptomatic at the time of diagnosis, though some may report symptoms of hyperglycemia, including polydipsia, polyuria, and blurred vision.
There is marked clinical heterogeneity in the presentation of T2DM.

The physical examination is usually normal, but fundoscopic examination may reveal signs of retinopathy (hard exudates, hemorrhages). If diabetes has gone undiagnosed for a prolonged period of time, signs of neuropathy may be present.

Monofilament, vibration, and superficial pain testing are all useful screening tests for diabetic neuropathy (with similar results to formal nerve conduction testing). Patients with an abnormal test result are 10 to 20 times more likely to have neuropathy. Using more than one test at a time does not add any value.
The presence of a carotid bruit on examination is associated with a 6.7-fold increased risk of stroke in the first 2 years of follow-up (95% CI, 3.0-14.9).
The three screening methods do not perform equally, with the OGTT being the most sensitive and hemoglobin A1c being the least sensitive.
ADA guidelines (2022) define T2DM as a reference laboratory A1c ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol), a fasting blood sugar ≥ 126 mg/dl (7.0 mmol/L), or a random blood sugar ≥ 200 mg/dl (11.1 mmol/L).

Only plasma glucose diagnostic tests (fasting plasma glucose, 2-hour oral glucose tolerance testing) should be used for diagnosis of T2DM in patients with increased red blood cell turnover (sickle cell disease, second/third trimesters of pregnancy, hemodialysis, recent blood loss/transfusion, erythropoietin therapy, etc.).

Sustained elevation in fasting blood glucose levels and 2-hour post-load glucose testing, even when below the threshold for a diabetes diagnosis, is significantly associated with future cardiovascular events and mortality. Current cut-offs for the diagnosis of T2DM are not based on cardiovascular disease predictions, but rather on the prevalence of retinopathy.

Do not use point-of-care A1c assays for diagnosis or screening due to inadequate accuracy. An exception are specific assays with FDA approval for diagnosis. Point-of-care A1c assays are more appropriately used for glucose monitoring in patients with pre-existing diabetes diagnoses.

When uncertainty exists regarding which type of diabetes a patient has, autoimmune markers associated with type 1 diabetes (e.g., autoantibodies to islet cells, GAD65, tyrosine phosphatases) can be tested for to help distinguish between the types. Recent trials have attempted to validate classification systems for subgroups of type 2 diabetes, however no recommendations have been made for clinical practice.

Several risk scores have been developed to assess risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus in asymptomatic patients. These risk scores are of uncertain clinical utility for clinicians who are already using USPSTF and/or ADA recommendations to guide their screening practices.

The FINDRISC/DRS was developed in 2003 in Finland, but has since been validated in multiple populations. In 2009, Bang, et al, published a table comparing characteristics and performance of various screening methods and predictive tools. The QDiabetes-2018 risk calculator was developed and validated by Hippisley-Cox and Coupland in the English primary care population to estimate a patient's 10 year risk of developing type 2. In total, there are 18 published risk tools for T2DM, but clinical relevance and utility are lacking.
The ADA recommends use of validated risk calculator (https://diabetes.org/socrisktest) or informal risk factor assessment to guide screening for prediabetes and T2DM in asymptomatic adults.

A meta-analysis of all published non-blood-based screening items resulted in a LR+ of 2.13, and LR- of 0.41. However, the combination of these non-blood-based screeners is not clinically available at this time. Use of non-laboratory methods for T2DM may be relevant in the future.

Patients can be tested for diabetes using hemoglobin A1c level (≥6.5%), fasting plasma glucose (≥126 mg/dL), the 2-hour 75 g glucose tolerance test (≥200 mg/dL), or random plasma glucose (≥200 mg/dL in the presence of suggestive symptoms).
Abnormal test results require a confirmation.

A hemoglobin A1c target between 7% and 8% appears reasonable for most patients with T2DM, but glycemic targets need to be individualized based on patient preference, comorbidities, polypharmacy risk, and life expectancy. Patients, especially older adults, who stay within their individualized A1c targets ≥60% of the time have lower all-cause mortality and cardiovascular complications than those who remain below and/or above their individualized targets ≥60% of the time. More intensive glycemic targets may reduce microvascular complications (eg, progression of microalbuminuria) but this is of questionable significance. B

A mainstay of non-pharmacologic therapy is referral to diabetes self-management education, either in group or individual treatment settings. This should be offered to all patients. B Referral for medical nutrition therapy is also recommended. C
Drug therapy should target blood pressure control, intensive lipid lowering, A and reasonable blood sugar control based on the patient's age and co-morbidities ().

Metformin is generally considered the first-line agent for glycemic control in T2DM. Additional agents such as sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists should be chosen based on individual patient needs. B
SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists should be strongly considered in T2DM patients with established ASCVD, CKD, CHF, or at high risk of CVD. A

If dual therapy with metformin plus another agent does not achieve glycemic goals, insulin may be considered. Long-acting insulin (eg, glargine, detemir) and NPH insulin have similar efficacy, but long-acting insulin is associated with less hypoglycemia whereas NPH insulin is more affordable. B
Statin therapy and smoking cessation improve cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in T2DM; these should be primary treatment goals (see ). A

Blood pressure should be lowered to less than 140/90, A and possibly less than 130/80. C A systolic blood pressure target of 120 mm Hg produces no additional cardiovascular benefits versus 140 mm Hg and increases harms. B
Patients with T2DM age 50-70 years and established CVD should receive aspirin. A It is less clear if other patients with T2DM benefit from aspirin therapy. B

Eight non-insulin hypoglycemic drug classes are available: biguanides, sulfonylureas, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, meglitinides, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors, and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists.

The American College of Physicians suggests aiming for an A1c level of 7% to 8% in most adults, and recommends deintensifying treatment for adults with an A1c of less than 6.5%. The ACP reviewed several published guidelines (AACE/ACE, ADA, ICSI, NICE, SIGN, VA/DoD) and major trials (ACCORD, ADVANCE, UKPDS 33 and 34, VADT) that invesitgate the effect of high versus low intensity A1c targets on various outcomes, including mortality. Tighter control leads to documented harms (including mortality in the ACCORD trial) and only small disease-oriented benefits, most notably non-fatal myocardial infarction.

For younger and healthier patients, tighter control may be beneficial. For older and frail patients, less tight control may be beneficial. This differs from ADA guidance of a glycemic goal of <7% for most adults without significant hypoglycemic risk.Glycemic targets need to be individualized based on patient preference, comorbidities, polypharmacy risk, and life expectancy.

Patients, especially older adults, who stay within their individualized HbA1c targets ≥60% of the time have lower all-cause mortality and cardiovascular complications than those who remain below and/or above their individualized targets ≥60% of the time. Furthermore, a large population-based cohort study showed that older adults whose cumulative glycemic control was greater than 9% over multiple decades were at greater risk of developing dementia. More intensive glycemic targets may reduce microvascular complications (eg, progression of microalbuminuria) but this is of questionable significance and may increase hypoglycemia.

First line therapy: Metformin is considered the first-line oral hypoglycemic agent for most adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus, including the 2023 ADA guidelines. The UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) 34 showed that metformin decreases all-cause mortality and long-term microvascular complications, although newer meta-analyses failed to confirm these benefits. The effects of metformin appear independent of the degree of glycemic control. Although metformin has long been contraindicated in diabetic patients with chronic kidney disease due to concerns about increasing the risk of lactic acidosis, there is little evidence that this adverse effect occurs in patients with mild to moderate CKD.

First line therapy with ASCVD, CKD or CHF: In these patients or at high risk of ASCVD (age >55 years with coronary, carotid, or lower extremity artery stenosis >50%, LVH), SGLT-2 inhibtors or GLP-1 receptor agonists should be strongly considered as either first-line or in addition to metformin therapy regardless of A1c. For patients with CKD (CrCl 30-60 ml/min) or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) or preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), SGLT-2 inhibtors lower hospitalizations for heart failure and are generally preferred. In addition, GLP-1 agonist semaglutide has proven benefit in HFpEF for reduced hospitalizations and should be considered.

Second line therapy: There is insufficient evidence to universally recommend a second oral hypoglycemic drug class after metformin; all classes had similar effects on hemoglobin A1c levels when compared in a network meta-analysis, though newer data indicates differences between classes and individual drugs in glycemic efficacy. ADA guidelines recommend an approach driven by co-morbidities and individual patient characteristics with most patients starting with metformin. This could include a sulfonylurea, thiazolidinedione, DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT-2 inhibitor, GLP-1 agonist, or basal insulin, with meglitinides and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors used less often due to convenience and lack of data on benefits. Factors to consider include cost, tolerability, renal risk, heart failure risk, and other cardiovascular risk. Insulin should be initiated in patients not reaching their treatment goals.

Relative efficacy: Though a network meta-analysis shows no difference in A1c reductions between classes, other evidence shows some differences. Metformin lowers A1c by 1% to 2% (dose-dependent effect), which is equivalent to the effect of sulfonylureas, meglitinides, thiazolidinediones and GLP-1 receptor agonists. DPP-4 inhibitors are less effective. SGLT-2 inhibitors lower A1c by about 0.5% compared to placebo. Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors lower A1c by 0.5% to 1%.In 2 separate network meta-analyses, DPP-4 inhibitors do not improve CV events, CV mortality, or all-cause mortality compared to placebo, while GLP-1 agonists and SGLT-2 inhibitors significantly improve all endpoints. A network meta-analysis found older treatments for T2DM, including metformin and insulin, do not affect patient-oriented outcomes. Only SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, and other cardiac-related problems.

listitem.strong: General principles of hypoglycemic drug therapy

list.listitem: Mortality reduction: Mortality reduction is the primary goal, with reduction in cardiovascular and renal events while avoiding adverse events are important secondary goals. Metformin, SGLT-2 inhibitors, and GLP-1 agonists decrease all-cause and cardiovascular mortality (effect not confirmed by meta-analysis for metformin/metformin+other medications). There are multiple RCT’s, meta-analyses and network meta-analyses on SGLT-2 and GLP-1 effects, with consistent, high quality evidence for mortality and other benefits. At the level of the individual drug, data is conflicting as to which drug gives which benefit. Mortality benefits were not confirmed in patients without baseline cardiovascular risk.

Practice guidelines published in BMJ make recommendations for treatment of T2DM based on the risk group:
Three or fewer cardiovascular risk factors without established CVD or CKD: Weak recommendation against starting SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists. More than three cardiovascular risk factors without established CVD or CKD: Weak recommendation for starting SGLT-2 inhibitors and weak against starting GLP-1 receptor agonists Established CVD or CKD: Weak recommendation for starting SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists Established CVD and CKD: Strong recommendation for starting SGLT-2 inhibitors and weak recommendation for starting GLP-1 receptor agonists For those committed to further reducing their risk for CVD and CKD outcomes: Weak recommendation for starting SGLT-2 inhibitors rather than GLP-1 receptor agonists.

Other benefits and harms: For non-insulin agents, see and . There are many carefully crafted, drug-company funded individual studies showing non-inferiority and benefit of individual drugs compared mostly to placebo, on various similar-but-not-identical composite outcome measures. Use caution when interpreting each study individually.

Use of insulin in patients with T2DM has not been shown to decrease cardiovascular or all-cause mortality despite reductions in blood sugar and hemoglobin A1c. There is an association with increased mortality and insulin use.An RCT enrolling 708 patients noted that the addition of once-daily basal insulin (detemir) to metformin and sulfonylurea may be less effective at lowering A1c than adding biphasic or prandial insulin. However, insulin detemir causes less weight gain and hypoglycemia.

A retrospective study of 25,489 patients with T2DM found NPH insulin to have equal efficacy and safety at less cost compared to long-acting insulin analogs. However, a Cochrane review comparing long-acting insulin (eg, glargine, detemir) and NPH insulin found similar efficacy between the two, but less hypoglycemia with long-acting insulin. Long-term efficacy and safety data is lacking to recommend short-acting insulin analogues versus regular human insulin. Insulin icodec is a once weekly basal insulin, not yet FDA approved. In an RCT it provided similar reduction in hemoglobin A1C to once daily insulin glargine in patients with poorly controlled T2DM. There was no difference in hypoglycemic events. The effect on cardiovascular and renal outomces is not known.
Continuing metformin when initiating insulin mitigates insulin-related weight gain without affecting glycemic control.
There is conflicting evidence regarding use of intermittently scanned continuous blood glucose monitoring for patients with T2DM on outcomes such as hypoglycemia and A1c control.

SGLT-2 inhibitors include canagliflozin, empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and ertugliflozin. Of the four, ertugliflozin has the least strong evidence of benefit. There are multiple RCTs, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses on combined cardiovascular outcomes, renal, and heart failure outcomes of SGLT-2 inhibitors. There is consistent high quality data showing positive class effect on all of these outcomes, but conflicting data between meta-analyses at the level of individual drug.Patients with established or higher risk of these co-morbidities consistently receive the most benefit, and patients at lower risk receive less or no benefit .

Use of an SGLT-2 reduces all-cause mortality, especially in persons with established ASCVD (NNT = 143). For progression of renal disease, the NNT is 67. For the outcome of major adverse cardiovascular events, the NNT = 167. For heart failure hospitalization, the NNT = 91. SGLT-2 inhibitors result in decreases in A1c, weight (mean 2 kg), and blood pressure (mean 5 mmHg).SGLT-2 benefits differ from GLP-1 benefits in that they offer renal protection and decreased risk of heart failure hospitalization. SGLT-2 offer no stroke prevention, whereas GLP-1 agonists do.

Per the ACP practice guidelines in 2024, clinicians should prioritize adding SGLT-2 inhibitors in patients with diabetes and comorbid CHF or CKD.SGLT-2 may reduce rates of atrial fibrillation in patients with T2DM, though this effect was not reproduced in other meta-analyses.SGLT-2 may provide similar benefits in older populations as compared to in persons younger than 65 years. However, a meta-analysis of frail adults or older adults with T2DM and heart failure that pooled data from disparate study designs found SGLT-2 to have little effect on glycemic control or all-cause mortality, but it appears to decrease cardiovascular deaths.

Potential harms: Canagliflozin and ertugliflozin may increase risk of amputation. SGLT-2 may increase risk of DKA compared to various controls, though data is conflicting. Retrospective studies show infection and insulin non-compliance as potential confounders for the development of DKA with SGLT-2 use.SGLT-2 increase the risk of genital infections.

An international guidelines suggest not using SGLT-2 inhibitors for patients with diabetes with low risk, to consider them for moderate risk patients, and strongly recommend them for high risk patients.

Several RCTs, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses show that GLP-1 receptor agonists have demonstrated a reduction in all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, non-fatal stroke, and non-fatal myocardial infarction in patients with T2DM and established CVD. Although the evidence for the beneficial effects of GLP-1 agonists on these outcomes as a class is consistent, there is some conflicting evidence between meta-analyses at the individual drug level.

CV benefits: Mixed evidence of CV benefit in patients without pre-existing ASCVD exists.The cardiovascular benefit of GLP-1 agonists in patients with T2DM appears consistent across subpopulations of age, sex, region, duration of diabetes, history of heart failure, BMI, A1c level, and estimated GFR.

Renal outcomes: GLP-1 agonists have been shown to reduce the risk of macroalbuminuria in patients with T2DM and CKD, but have not been shown to delay progression of diabetic kidney disease in terms of eGFR, ESRD, and renal death.

Heart failure: GLP-1 agonists have not consistently shown a protective effect on hospitalization for heart failure in patients with T2DM, but a recent trial of semaglutide lowered risk of heart failure hospitalization in patients with preserved ejection fraction.

Weight loss: The STEP-1 trial compared lifestyle interventions with semaglutide 2.4mg weekly, with an added weight loss of approximately 30 pounds and >50% showing a reduction of 15% body weight. Tirzepatide 10mg and 15mg weekly has shown increased percentage of weight loss indirectly compared to semaglutide.

Per the ACP practice guidelines released in 2024, clinicians should prioritize adding GLP-1 agonists in patients with diabetes who are at an increased risk of stroke or who have a goal of total body weight loss. A randomized trial of 5047 patients taking metformin and randomized to the GLP-1 agonist liraglutide, insulin, glimepiride, or the DPP-4 inhibitor sitagliptin as a second drug found the most favorable cardiovascular outcomes with liraglutide.
An international guidelines suggest not using GLP-1 agonists for patients with diabetes with low risk, to consider them for moderate risk patients, and strongly recommend them for high risk patients.

Clinical guidelines released by the American College of Physicians (ACP) in 2024 recommend against adding a DPP-4 inhibitor as a second-line hypoglycemic agent in adults with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycemic control to reduce morbidity and all cause mortality. The meta-analyses sugget that DPP-4 inhibitors may increase hospitalizations due to CHF and likely also increase the risk for major adverse cardiac events, and progression of CKD when compared to SGLT-2 inhibitors.

The assumption that diabetes alone is a heart disease risk factor equivalent to prior myocardial infarction has been questioned.

Hyperlipidemia: Statins delay first myocardial infarction independent of LDL levels in patients with diabetes. Fenofibrate appears to decrease the need for photocoagulation but does not prevent coronary events in diabetics; thus, statins are the first-line treatment for lipid-lowering.

Hypertension: Blood pressure should be lowered to less than 140/90 per JNC-8 guidelines or less than 130/80 per the 2017 ACC/AHA (provided 10-year ASCVD risk is >10%). ESC/ESH 2018 and ESC/EASD 2019 Guidelines advocate for individualized blood pressure goals depending on age, cardiovascular risk, and renal disease. More intensive blood pressure control increases adverse effects (NNH 50 over 5 years). All anti-hypertensive drug classes are effective first-line agents, and combination therapy is usually required. ACEi/ARBs reduce progression of albuminuria, while ACEi's also reduce mortality. Calcium channel blockers are less effective than ACE inhibitors in preventing nephropathy progression, and they may increase the risk of myocardial infarction (NNH = 11). Beta-blockers are safe and effective for older patients with diabetes after acute myocardial infarction; physicians should feel comfortable prescribing these medications for the elderly. ACE inhibitor plus ARB increases the risk for advancement to dialysis.

Aspirin: Patients with T2DM age 50 to 70 with known cardiovascular disease benefit from aspirin therapy, in accordance with ACC/AHA. Patients with T2DM and other cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, smoking, dyslipidemia, family history, or albuminuria) may also benefit from low dose aspirin, though risk versus benefit must be considered. Benefit is low for patients less than 50 years old, and bleeding risk is high for patients over 70 years old; clinical judgment is advised in these groups. Data from the ASCEND trial show a very small benefit vs risk margin for patients with diabetes over the age of 40, driven mostly by a reduction in TIA's and revascularization.

Retrospective analysis of Medicare recipients suggest mortality disparities by race in diabetic patients with co-morbid conditions: Black and American Indian/ Alaska Natives had higher mortality compared to white patients. Hispanic patients had similar mortality to white patients. Black patients, elderly patients, publicly insured patients, and patients with cardiovascular and renal comorbidities are less likely to be prescribed an SGLT-2 as compared to younger, non-Black, commercially insured, healthier populations.Meta-analyses question the efficacy of GLP-1 agonist and SGLT-2 inhibitor in non-White and female populations. Evidence is inconclusive, likely due to under-representation of these groups in clinical studies. We strongly caution against using this data to discourage use of otherwise evidence-based, life-saving interventions in populations who already face health disparities.
Surgical debridement of diabetic foot ulcers does not improve healing. Hydrogels are better than gauze dressings.

Based on low-certainty evidence from a Cochrane review, hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) may improve healing of diabetic foot ulcers in the short-term but not long-term. A guideline for critical limb ischemia noted the short-term benefits of HBOT in patients with T2DM and arterial ulcers, but pointed out that HBOT is not a substitue for revascularization. Adding HBOT to usual care does not appear to have beneficial effects on wound healing or limb salvage outcomes, based on a European multicenter RCT evaluating patients with T2DM and arterial ulcers.

Bariatric surgery facilitates weight loss and improved glycemic control, but has not yet been shown to decrease all-cause mortality. One retrospective study of patients with T2DM with obesity showed lower major adverse cardiac events for bariatric surgery compared to GLP-1 agonists. Rates of other non-cardiovascular adverse events appear higher with bariatric surgery compared to medical management.
Sleeve gastrectomy is not equivalent to gastric bypass for the measures of weight loss and diabetes remission at 5 years.

Chinese herbal medicines (holy basil leaves, Xianzhen Pian, Qidan Tongmai, traditional Chinese formulae, Huoxue Jiangtang Pingzhi, and Inolter) show hypoglycemic effects in patients with type 2 diabetes. Further high-quality studies are needed prior to widespread use.

Fish oil lowers triglycerides in patients with type 2 diabetes but may raise LDL cholesterol levels. It has no significant effect on glycemic control and has not been shown to affect vascular events or mortality.
Vitamin E supplements are no better than placebo for relief of diabetic peripheral neuropathy symptoms.
Zinc supplementation has been proposed for the prevention of diabetes because of its role in insulin synthesis, but no evidence currently supports its use.
Low quality evidence gives conflicting results for the effect of tai chi and qigong on glycemic control.
Cinnamon comsumption has not been proven to reduce hemoglobin A1c significantly, but may reduce fasting glucose levels .
Omega-3 (dietary or supplemental) has no effect on glycemic control (moderate quality evidence).
Evidence for the effects of alpha-linolenic acid, polyunsaturated fat, and omega-6 on glycemic control is inconclusive due to low/very low quality, but points to no effect.
EDTA chelation does not appear effective in reducing adverse cardiovascular events in adults with T2DM and history of MI.

Based on data from systematic review evaluating RCTs with low risk of bias, therapeutic footwear that purposely offloads plantar pressure and that is consistently worn by the patient prevents recurrent diabetic foot ulcers.

Both group-based and individual diabetes self-management education is associated with reductions in hemoglobin A1c, systolic blood pressure, body weight, cost, all-cause mortality and the need for diabetic medications. ADA guidelines suggest providing referral to diabetes self-management education and medical nutrition therapy for all patients with type 2 diabetes.Some evidence suggests that education provided by formally trained diabetes educators (dieticians, pharmacists, and nurses) is more effective than in-office dietary advice for short-term measures such as HbA1c, weight, and lipids. There is inadequate data on longer-term outcomes, such as hospital admission rates and quality of life.
Patient education seems to improve knowledge and self-reported foot care behaviors, but there is insufficient evidence that it prevents diabetic foot ulcerations.
There are many diabetes self-management apps available on smart phones, however, quality assurance mechanisms to ensure appropriate warnings and advice are often lacking.

Weight-loss strategies targeting diet, physical activity, or behavioral interventions result in modest weight loss in comparison with usual care. Up to 12 percent of participants in an intensive lifestyle intervention achieved complete or partial remission of diabetes 1 to 4 years after the start of the intervention. Changes in hemoglobin A1c correspond with weight loss. See chapter on Obesity and weight loss (adult).

Even without weight loss, exercise significantly improves glycemic control and plasma triglycerides (but not blood pressure or total cholesterol) in patients with type 2 diabetes. Lifestyle interventions combining exercise and dietary portion control also reduce disability and improve mobility and physical fitness in adults with type 2 diabetes.

In a well-designed RCT of 5145 adults followed for a median of 9.6 years, patients who received an intensive lifestyle intervention including exercise and diet components had similar rates of all-cause mortality and a composite measure of cardiovascular outcomes as patients receiving usual care.

A primary-care administered food-replacement program in the UK resulted in increased weight loss, diabetes remission, and increased quality of life as compared to usual care. Adoption in clincial settings will likely be limited by high drop-out rates in the original study group, cost, and availability.
Moderate quality evidence shows short-term glycemic improvement with periodontal disease treatment.
Type 2 diabetics may require hospitalization for hyperglycemic crises (most commonly hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state but also diabetic ketoacidosis).
Sildenafil triples the likelihood of successful intercourse in diabetic men with erectile dysfunction.
Gabapentin and amitriptyline are equally effective for the relief of pain from diabetic neuropathy with equivalent discontinuation rates. Amitriptyline costs significantly less.

American College of Cardiology / American Heart Association recommend GLP-1 agonists and SGLT-2 inhibitors in diabetic patients with established CV disese to prevent major adverse cardiovascular events.

In diabetics with microalbuminuria, overt proteinuria, or elevated creatinine, ACE inhibitors and ARBs are effective in slowing the progression of disease. ARBs have no advantage over ACE inhibitors and should be used only in patients who cannot tolerate the less-expensive ACE inhibitors. Combining an ACE inhibitor and ARB increases the risk for hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury but does not improve cardiovascular outcomes or mortality. SGLT-2 inhibitors have also been shown to reduce the risk of progression of chronic kidney disease in patients with T2DM and albuminuric CKD. Dapagliflozin decreased all-cause mortality, need for dialysis, or renal transplant in CKD patients, including diabetic patients, compared to placebo.
High-dose B vitamins are ineffective in slowing nephropathy and increase adverse cardiovascular outcomes and all-cause mortality (NNH = 11).
KDIGO recommends ACE/ARBs and tobacco cessation in diabetic patients with albuminuria. Diabetic patients with CKD should consider SGLT-2 inhibitors to prevent progression of disease.

Finerenone, a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, may improve renal outcomes in type 2 diabetic patients with CKD, and decrease hospitalization for heart failure. Patients in these studies were not on SGLT-2 inhibitors.

In carefully crafted studies funded by the drug manufacturers, SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists decreased composite renal outcomes in patients with T2DM and renal disease, cardiovascular disease, or cardiovascular risk factors. This was mostly driven by incidence of proteinuria. These studies have been criticized for sources of bias, risks of side effects, high cost of the medications, and high NNT's. Of note, none are head-to-head evaluations between the study drug and established "gold standard" T2DM treatments such as metformin--the only direct comparator was placebo. The ADA recommends use of these two drug classes to prevent worsening of renal disease in patients with T2DM and chronic kidney disease (A recommendation). A recent network meta-analysis confirms the effect of SGLT-2 inhibitors on renal outcomes, albeit with low confidence in the effect estimate.
SGLT-2 inhibitors decrease hospitalization for heart failure in patients with pre-existing heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (<30%), including patients with type 2 diabetes.
Complications of type 2 diabetes stem from glucotoxicity to multiple organ systems and tissues, and primarily include nephropathy, retinopathy, and neuropathy.
For hospitalized patients with diabetes, care by a diabetes team improves metabolic control and reduces length of stay.
Insulin and other medications need to be adjusted in hospitalized patients with diabetes; guidelines are based on expert opinion only.
For diabetics admitted for acute myocardial infarction, intensive control of blood glucose does not improve short-term or long-term mortality.
Strict blood sugar control for patients in intensive care units increases mortality.
Microalbuminuria may not be a good predictor of diabetic nephropathy. Screening for urine microalbumin has not been shown to decrease progression to end-stage renal disease or dialysis. B
In T2DM, self glucose monitoring does not improve A1c levels and leads to more symptomatic hypoglycemic events. A

For type 2 diabetics with a normal baseline eye examination result, 5.3% will develop any type of retinopathy in the next year. The majority of retinopathy will be mild, with only 0.3% developing sight-threatening diabetic retinopathy (95% CI, 0.1%-0.5%). Patients with an abnormal baseline examination result have a more rapid rate of progression.

Despite some conflicting data, it appears that patients with diabetes have lower cardiovascular and mortality risk than patients with previous myocardial infarction. This may have clinical relevance to initiation of statins and aspirin for young patients with T2DM and few other cardiovascular risk factors.

Microalbuminuria may not be a good predictor of eventual development of diabetic nephropathy. In 1 small study, only 6% of patients with microalbuminuria progressed to diabetic nephropathy, while 17% of patients without microalbuminuria developed nephropathy.
For patients with diabetic foot ulcers, demonstration of intact vascular supply with an audible pulse by Doppler predicts healing.

Patients with T2DM have a 2-fold increased risk of developing Alzheimer disease as compared to the non-diabetic population. Additionally, adults 50 years and older with T2DM with long-term average HbA1c >9% have a higher risk of dementia (hazard ratios [HRs] 1.31-1.74). Use of metformin, DPP4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and SGLT-2 inibitors are associated with decreased risk of dementia as compared to other patients with T2DM.

For men and women age 50 and older with T2DM, the overall life expectancy is approximately 8 years less than men and women without diabetes. Men and women with T2DM also develop cardiovascular disease approximately 8 years earlier than do patients with out T2DM.
In one large cohort study, at age 60 years, all-cause mortality for patients with T2DM was 15.6 per 1000 person-years, as compared to 6.8 per 1000 person-years for patients without diabetes.

Social determinants of health are increasingly recognized as a source of inequities in diabetes care. Factors affecting outcomes include socioeconomic status, housing, environmental toxins, insurance status, and others. Examples of successful interventions include health literacy work, community health workers, and Medicaid expansion.
Follow-up for patients with diabetes should include regular assessment of blood pressure, lipids, and screening for tobacco use.

Expert guidelines suggest intervals for checking hemoglobin A1c levels, nephropathy screening, retinopathy screening, and neuropathy screening. However, rapid testing of hemoglobin A1c in the office does not save money or improve glycemic control compared with usual care.

Although hemoglobin A1c correlates with mean plasma glucose, reaching a goal hemoglobin A1c of 7.0% (tight control) is not associated with improvements in cardiovascular outcomes or mortality rates when compared with usual care (mean A1c of 7.9%). In trials that suggest an association between lower hemoglobin A1c and improved outcomes, hemoglobin A1c may be a marker for compliance with all treatments (lipid-lowering, smoking cessation, and blood pressure control).

Screening for microalbuminuria has not been shown to decrease or delay progression of diabetic nephropathy to end-stage renal disease. Dipstick for proteinuria may be an alternative, although treating all diabetics with an ACE inhibitor is more cost-effective than screening for either microalbuminuria or macroalbuminuria. Given the slow rate of progression of retinopathy in diabetics with a normal baseline examination result, it is reasonable to decrease the frequency of dilated eye examinations as long as results remain normal.

In patients with type 2 diabetes, self-monitoring of blood glucose does not improve hemoglobin A1c levels and increases symptomatic hypoglycemic events (NNTH = 6). Self-monitoring of blood glucose might be effective in other situations (type 1 or poorly controlled type 2 patients), but studies are limited.

Continuous glucose monitoring versus traditional fingersticks in type 2 diabetes has conflicting results with HbA1c lowering. One study of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c >9%) on prandial insulin resulted in a greater reduction in HbA1c compared to self monitoring at 8 months (8.0% vs 8.4%). Two other studies of type 2 DM patients on insulin have not resulted in significant HbA1c lowering at 6 months.A 2024 study by the ADA corroborated prior findings and further demonstrated that both intermittent and continuous glucose monitors are associated with increased risk of adverse effects including, but not limited to, psychological distress.

The ADA recommends testing overweight children for diabetes every 2 years starting at age 10 if they have 2 of the following risk factors: family history of diabetes, non-white race, signs of insulin resistance, or maternal history of gestational diabetes.
Evidence to guide treatment of T2DM in children is limited; consensus guidelines based only on expert opinion are available.
See for pediatric risk factors for T2DM.

Management of pre-existing diabetes in pregnancy includes optimal glucose control, which involves diet, exercise, and medical therapy. Long-acting insulin is the preferred therapy, with intensification when needed. For patients unable or unwilling to use insulin, metformin may be considered during pregnancy. However, the addition of metformin to insulin to treat pregnant patients with early onset gestational diabetes or preexisting T2DM does not appear to prevent preterm preeclampsia.
Detemir compared to NPH in type 2 diabetic pregnant patients may result in improved neonatal and maternal outcomes. More studies are needed.

feature.caption: Hypoglycemic Agents for Type 2 Diabetes.
feature.feature_body:
Medication Evidence of Efficacy /Benefit Evidence of Harm
Metformin - Decreases cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality, independent of glycemic control, but not confirmed in 2 meta-analysis - weight neutral/benefit - no hypoglycemia - No increase in lactic acidosis if used as prescribed for patients without risk factors for lactic acidosis - Safe for patients with heart failured-f - frequent GI side effects
Sulfonylureas - May decrease microvascular complications but has not been shown to improve all-cause mortality,* and may increase mortality - Weight gain - Risk of hypoglycemia - Increased risk of cancer-related death compared with patients treated with metformin - conflicting data about use in heart failure, but worse than metformin
SGLT-2 Inhibitors; https://www.fda.gov/Drugs/DrugSafety/ucm557507.htm; https://www.fda.gov/Drugs/DrugSafety/ucm475463.htm - Weight loss - Lower blood pressure - Improved mortality in patients with CVD (empagliflozin, canagliflozin) - benefit in heart failure - prevents nephropathy progression - minimal hypoglycemia (no major events) - Genitourinary infections - Volume depletion, dizziness - FDA warning: amputation (canagliflozin) - fractures - FDA warning: euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis
GLP-1 Agonists - Weight loss - improved all-cause mortality & non-fatal stroke - prevents nephropathy progression (liraglutide, semaglutide) - minimal hypoglycemia (no major events) - GI upset - FDA warning: theoretical risk of thyroid C-cell tumors (animal studies) - Injectable - semaglutide worse than placebo for retinopathy - pancreatitis
DPP-4 Inhibitor; https://www.fda.gov/Drugs/DrugSafety/ucm486096.htm - prevents nephropathy progression (linagliptin) - minimal hypoglycemia (no major events) - FDA warning: CHF (saxagliptin, alogliptin) - possible risk of pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer
Meglitinides - minimal hypoglycemia (no major events) - weight gain - GI upset (less than metformin)
Thiazolidinediones - possible CV mortality benefit (not consistent) but not all-cause mortality - minimal hypoglycemia (no major events) - Weight gain - edema - FDA warning: CHF exacerbations, contraindicated if NYHA class II-IV HF
Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors - no hypoglycemia - GI upset - three times daily dosing
Insulin - greatest glycemic effect - Weight gain - major hypoglycemia - Increased mortality - possible increased cancer-related mortality but inconsistent data
*UKPDS 33 was comparison of intensive vs conventional glucose control. Some patients in the control group received SU's as well; unclear if difference in groups was due to glucose control (original study design) or SU specifically

feature.caption: Risk Factors for Development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
feature.feature_body:
Risk Factors
First-degree relative with diabetes High-risk race/ethnicity (e.g., African-American, Latino, Native American, Asian American, Pacific Islander) Women who were diagnosed with gestational diabetes History of CVD Hypertension HDL <35 mg/dL or triglycerides >250 mg/dL Women with PCOS Physical inactivity Other clinical conditions associated with T2DM (severe obesity, acanthosis nigricans) Low dietary flavonoid intake (found in commonly-consumed vegetables and fruits, tea, grains, and cocoa* Antipsychotic use Statin use**
*NOT an ADA defined risk factor but evidence shows association **Not established as a causation but consideration should be taken when deciding whether or not to screen
